ch000.anchor: a single scale and half a claw
ch000.note: The book's title, Shanghai linzhao (上海鱗爪), means literally "the scales and claws of Shanghai": the odd fragments by which a whole beast may be guessed at. The preface plays on the same figure, yi lin ban zhao (一鱗半爪), "a single scale and half a claw," a set phrase for a mere glimpse of the whole.

Geyan congji (格言叢輯), a compilation of improving sayings here credited to Yu Muxia. Its authorship, its vogue among warlord-era troops, and its twenty volumes of sequels rest on this preface's own account; I have found no independent record of the work, and it should be read as the prefacer's claim for his friend, not as established fact.

From the "Heaven and Earth" (Tiandi) chapter of the Zhuangzi. The point of the quoted lines is that grand, refined music means nothing to the villager's ear, while a common ditty sets him laughing and clapping, so a writer who would reach ordinary people must speak in their key.
Zheyang (折楊) and Huanghua (皇荂), the two tune-titles Zhuangzi names, were popular folk airs, the vulgar songs set against the "grand music" no villager can take in.

ch000.anchor: keeping one's aim low and forgoing lofty talk
ch000.note: Bei zhi wu shen gaolun (卑之毋甚高論). The words are Emperor Wen of Han's to his official Zhang Shizhi (as recorded in the Shiji and Hanshu): keep to what is concrete and workable now, with no high-flown theorizing. The phrase later became a modest way of saying that one is offering nothing lofty, only plain good sense.

The pen name of Chen Diexian (陳蝶仙, 1879–1940), a leading novelist of the "Mandarin Ducks and Butterflies" school, an editor of the Shenbao's literary supplement, and the industrialist who founded Household Industries (家庭工業社), maker of the Butterfly-brand toothpowder. He wrote this preface as the author's friend.
The Double Seventh (七夕, Qixi), the seventh night of the seventh lunar month, falling in late summer. In the sexagenary cycle the year guiyou (癸酉) here is 1933, which dates the preface.

ch001.note: The Republic adopted the Gregorian solar calendar as its guoli or "national calendar" on 1 January 1912, but the old lunar calendar kept its hold on daily life. After the Nationalists made Nanjing their capital in 1927 the government pressed the point hard, ordering in 1928 that almanacs drop the lunar dates and campaigning until about 1930 to abolish the traditional lunar New Year in favour of a "National Calendar New Year." The drive proved unenforceable, which is the very stalemate this sketch describes.

The reckoning is loose and runs a little ahead of the book. Twenty-four years from the 1912 adoption of the solar calendar points to about 1936, and "seven or eight" years from the 1927 move to Nanjing to about 1934–35, whereas the collection was first published in 1933. The sketch may belong to a later printing, or the author is simply counting in round numbers; I have not been able to collate this 2019 reprint against the 1933 edition.

Xie nian (謝年), the year-end thanksgiving: a household sets out fish and meat, lights red candles and incense, kowtows and lets off firecrackers to thank its gods for the year's protection before the New Year comes in.

ch001.anchor: the eight festivals of the year
ch001.note: The "four seasons and eight festivals" (四時八節), the eight seasonal turning-points of the farmer's year, the solstices and equinoxes and the days that open each season, at which offerings were customarily made.
The phrase echoes the Analects, shen zhong zhui yuan (慎終追遠), "tend the rites of death with care and honour the distant dead," the classical ground of ancestral sacrifice.

Nianguan (年關), the year's end pictured as a gate or pass that every account must clear. Debts run up with shops and with the native banks (錢莊, the traditional Chinese money-shops that supplied most commercial credit) had by custom to be paid off in full before the New Year, on pain of ruined standing.

ch001.anchor: the City God Temple in the Nanshi
ch001.note: The Old City God Temple (老城隍廟) in Shanghai's walled Chinese city, founded in the early fifteenth century; its enshrined City God is Qin Yubai (秦裕伯, c.1295–1373), a Yuan–Ming official canonized as the city's tutelary spirit. The temple and its bazaar were a great popular resort.

ch001.anchor: the Hong Temple on Nanjing Road
ch001.note: The Hong Temple (虹廟), properly the Bao'an Situ Temple (保安司徒廟) at what is now 496 East Nanjing Road, a temple to Guanyin famous for its thick incense-smoke and long a resort of Shanghai's courtesans, who came to pray for luck in their trade.

Tou xiang (頭香), the merit of being the very first to set incense before the god as the New Year opens, thought to win the year's best fortune, which is why, as the author says, the competing worshippers keep pushing the hour earlier and earlier.
Gongxi facai (恭喜發財), "congratulations and may you grow rich," still the standard New Year greeting; the second phrase, xinnian deyi (新年得意), wishes one a year that goes one's way.

Yuanbao cha (元寶茶), New Year tea served with two olives floating on the lid, the olives standing in for silver ingots (元寶) as a wish for wealth. The red-paper "tea packet" (茶包) handed to the departing guest is a cash tip for the host's servants.

The money runs in silver dollars and their fractions. A dollar (塊 or 元, the silver yuan) divided into ten mao (毛, also jiao), each of ten cents; "small silver" (小洋) meant the subsidiary coin, which passed at a slight discount to the big standard dollar (大洋). Four mao is thus about forty cents.

Yasui qian (壓歲錢), the New Year cash an elder gives a child "to weigh down the year": by a pun on sui, it presses down the sui (祟) demon and buys the child a safe year. The word in the text is the Shanghai form yasui dian (壓歲鈿), dian being the Wu-dialect word for money.

The foreign concessions, the International Settlement and the French Concession, each self-governing with its own by-laws and its own police force (the buhang or station-house). A street pedlar needed a licence and could be run in for trading where the rules forbade.

Jie caishen (接財神). In the Jiangnan region the God of Wealth is the "road-head god" (路頭神), and he is commonly met on the fifth day of the first lunar month, reckoned his birthday, though some traditions place it on the second. Households vie to receive him first, meeting him on the eve of the fourth as here, a custom known as "grabbing the road-head" (搶路頭); it is recorded in the Qing handbook Qing jia lu.

Juan pugai zou lu (捲舖蓋走路), to be sacked and sent packing. The mordant point is that the year's welcoming-rite doubled as the reckoning at which a shop decided which of its clerks would be kept on (蟬聯) for the coming year and which turned out.
Gaosheng (高升), a firecracker that shoots up whistling before it bursts; the name puns on "rising high," a New Year good-luck word.
Suo lishi qian (索利市錢). Lishi (利市) is a lucky opening handout, the small cash given for good fortune at the New Year; the roving bands demanded it with gong and drum, a festive shakedown.

ch002.note: Song Jiaoren (1882-1913), of Taoyuan in Hunan, was the chief organizer of the Kuomintang, which he built in 1912 by merging the revolutionary Tongmenghui with several small parties, and the leading advocate of responsible cabinet government. His party's sweep of the 1912-13 parliamentary elections put him in line to become premier; he was shot days later. (Corroborated: English and Chinese Wikipedia, Song Jiaoren.)

The Minli Bao (1910-1913), founded in Shanghai by Yu Youren, was the most influential revolutionary daily of the late Qing and the organ of the Tongmenghui in central China; Song Jiaoren was among its writers.

Yu Youren (1879-1964): founder of the Minli Bao and its sister papers, later a Kuomintang elder who presided over the Control Yuan for thirty-four years, and one of the most admired calligraphers of the age.

ch002.anchor: Yuan Shikai held the reins of state
ch002.note: On Yuan Shikai, see the Glossary. As provisional president from 1912 he steadily undercut the Republic's parliamentary constitution, the course Song Jiaoren rose to oppose.

The book says Song declined this post; in fact he took it, in Tang Shaoyi's first Republican cabinet (April 1912), and resigned in July 1912 in protest at Yuan's conduct. What he later refused were Yuan's private offers of office and money. (Contradicted: Chinese Wikipedia, Song Jiaoren; the book conflates the two.)

ch002.anchor: destroy Song and be rewarded for the merit
ch002.note: These four characters (hui Song chou xun) really were the cant of the case: after the shooting, a cache of coded telegrams was seized at Ying Guixin's house and published, among them Hong Shuzu's wire to Ying using this very phrase, and Ying's reply invoking the Liangshan outlaws. (Corroborated: Chinese Wikipedia, Song Jiaoren.)

ch002.anchor: the twentieth of March, in the second year of the Republic
ch002.note: That is, 20 March 1913. Song was shot at the platform of the Shanghai North Station about 10:40 that night and died of the wound early on 22 March. (Corroborated.)

Huang Xing (1874-1916), styled Keqiang, here written Kexing; the foremost military leader of the 1911 Revolution and, with Sun Yat-sen, a founder of the Kuomintang. He was traveling with Song and was unhurt.
The Shanghai North Railway Station (Zhabei), terminus of the Shanghai-Nanjing line.
Thirty-two by the Chinese count, which reckons a person one year old at birth; by Western reckoning Song was thirty (born April 1882).

The failed Nationalist rising against Yuan Shikai in the summer of 1913, provoked by Song's murder and by Yuan's unauthorized foreign loan. Its defeat left Yuan supreme and drove Sun Yat-sen and his followers into exile.

Zhao Bingjun (1859-1914), Yuan's premier and interior minister, named as the case's principal after the telegrams surfaced. He was made military governor of Zhili and died suddenly at Tianjin in February 1914, bleeding from the orifices; the traditional account holds he was poisoned on Yuan's order, though some later scholars ascribe it to a stroke. (Chinese sources; the poisoning is the standard allegation, not settled fact.)

Ying Guixin, the Shanghai gangland go-between who hired the gunman. He escaped after the case collapsed and was murdered in a first-class railway carriage between Beijing and Tianjin in January 1914. (Corroborated.)

Hong Shuzu, Zhao Bingjun's secretary in the interior ministry, who relayed the orders to Ying by telegram. He hid in the German leasehold at Qingdao until Yuan's death, was seized in 1917, and was executed in 1919 (see the note below on the manner of it).
Wu Shiying, the hired gunman, a rough character ignorant of whom he served. Arrested at once, he died in prison on 24 April 1913, widely believed poisoned to keep him from testifying. (Corroborated.)

The system Song championed: a cabinet drawn from and answerable to the majority party in parliament, which would have made the elected assembly, not the president, the seat of power. It was exactly this that Yuan meant to prevent.
An allusion to the outlaw band of Mount Liang in the novel Water Margin; in the plotters' telegrams it stood, in code, for the revolutionaries to be put down.

ch002.anchor: hunting his men as one hunts a horse by its portrait
ch002.note: Rendering the idiom an tu suo ji, 'to seek a fine horse by its picture', that is, to go strictly by a likeness; here doubly apt, since the names on the photograph had been switched.

Cheng Dequan (1860-1930), military governor of Jiangsu in 1913, who pressed for the case to be tried at law; it was under his authority that the arrests were made and the incriminating papers seized. (Corroborated.)

ch002.anchor: poisoned Wu Shiying in his cell
ch002.note: Wu did die in his cell (24 April 1913), and the poisoning to silence him is the standard account; the book's tale of an agent named Long is the popular embroidery of it.

The book's 'electric garrote' is not borne out by the record: Hong Shuzu was condemned by the Supreme Court in Beijing and hanged on 5 April 1919. The hanging is famous for having gone wrong, the drop nearly tearing his heavy body's head from its shoulders. (The method was judicial hanging; the 'electric' detail is unverified embroidery.)

ch002.anchor: the Minli, the Tianduo, the Minquan, the Zhonghua Min
ch002.note: Four revolutionary Shanghai dailies of the early Republic: the Minli Bao (see above); the Tianduo Bao; the Minquan Bao (see the next note); and the Zhonghua Minbao, founded 1912 and shut after the Second Revolution. All were violently anti-Yuan.

ch002.anchor: The Minquan Bao was the fiercest
ch002.note: The Minquan Bao (Shanghai, 1912-13) was the most radical of the anti-Yuan sheets, made notorious by Dai Jitao's editorials; see also the chapters on Dai's arrest and on Zhou Hao.

Zhou Hao, styled Shaoheng, the paper's director; he is the subject of a later chapter of his own. Reliable histories credit the Minquan Bao's audacity chiefly to Dai Jitao's pen; the anecdotes of Zhou's personal daring rest largely on accounts like this one.

ch003.anchor: Dai Jitao, President of the Examination Yuan
ch003.note: On Dai, see the Glossary. When this was written he headed the Examination Yuan, one of the five branches of the Nationalist government (charged with the civil-service examinations); in 1912 he was still the young tabloid firebrand 'Tianchou'.

Tianchou means 'heaven's vengeance' or 'sworn foe of the age'; a fitting signature for his slashing anti-Yuan editorials, and the name later given to the collection of them (see the following chapter).

ch003.anchor: the great loan of the Republic's first year
ch003.note: The great foreign 'Reorganization Loan' that Yuan's government negotiated with a banking consortium to fund itself outside parliament; concluded in April 1913, it was a chief grievance of the revolutionaries and helped touch off the Second Revolution.

The record dates and motivates the arrest differently: on 20 May 1912 Dai published a signed piece titled 'Kill' in the Minquan Bao, calling for the deaths of Yuan and others; the International Settlement authorities arrested him for incitement on 22 May and released him on bail the next day. The book's version, an arrest at Yuan's own instance over the loan editorials, telescopes this. (Chinese Wikipedia, Dai Jitao.)

ch003.anchor: the Central Police Station on Fourth Avenue
ch003.note: Fourth Avenue is the popular name of Fuzhou Road; the Central (Louza) Police Station of the International Settlement's Municipal Police stood on it.
The Mixed Court of the International Settlement, where a Chinese magistrate sat with a foreign assessor to try Chinese defendants in the concession; the ordinary forum for a case like this.

ch004.note: A real book: the collected editorials of Dai Jitao ('Dai Tianchou'), gathered from the Minquan Bao and much read by young radicals. (Corroborated: it survives as the Dai Tianchou wenji.)

ch004.anchor: the pictorial of the Dagonghe Bao
ch004.note: The Dagonghe Bao (Republican Daily) was a Shanghai paper of the opposing, pro-Yuan camp; its cartoon, setting the book's title behind a dog, is the joke the chapter's own title picks up, that the collection was so much dog's wind.

ch005.note: Cai Yuanpei (1868-1940), revolutionary and educator, later the first minister of education of the Republic and the reforming chancellor of Peking University; in these years a leader of the Shanghai Patriotic School circle around the Subao.
Wu Zhihui (1865-1953), classical scholar and anarchist-leaning revolutionary, later a Kuomintang elder; a fellow of Cai's in the Subao circle.

The Subao, a Shanghai daily radicalized in 1903, when it praised Zou Rong's tract and printed Zhang Taiyan's essay reviling the Guangxu Emperor. Its actual editor was Zhang Shizhao, not Zhang Taiyan; the book makes Zhang Taiyan and Zou Rong its 'chief and deputy editors', which telescopes the roles of writers and editor.

ch005.anchor: In the thirty-second year of Guangxu
ch005.note: That is, 1906. The date is the book's error: the Subao case actually broke in the summer of 1903 (Guangxu 29). 1906 is rather the year Zhang Taiyan finished his term and left for Japan. (Chinese Wikipedia, Subao case.)

The foreign-run prison of the International Settlement (the Ward Road Gaol); a 'Western' gaol because it lay under concession, not Chinese, authority. Tried in the Settlement's Mixed Court, Zhang and Zou served their terms there.

Zou Rong (1885-1905), the young Sichuanese author of The Revolutionary Army, sentenced to two years in the Subao case; he died in the Western Gaol in April 1905, before his term was out. (Corroborated.)
The Aisin Gioro clan, the Manchu imperial house of the Qing dynasty.

ch006.note: The coup of 1898 (the wuxu year) that ended the Hundred Days' Reform, when the Empress Dowager Cixi seized power, imprisoned the Guangxu Emperor, and had the leading reformers killed or driven abroad.

ch006.anchor: old Mr. Kang was truly the moving spirit
ch006.note: On Kang Youwei, see the Glossary. He was the reform movement's chief ideologue and the emperor's adviser in the Hundred Days.
Kang Guangren (1867-1898), Kang Youwei's younger brother, one of the 'Six Gentlemen of Wuxu' beheaded at Caishikou after the coup.

Two more of the Six Gentlemen executed at Caishikou, the Beijing execution ground, in September 1898. Tan Sitong (1865-1898) is the most celebrated of them, having refused to flee, saying the reform must have its martyr.

The Baohuang Hui, or Protect-the-Emperor Society, which Kang and Liang built among overseas Chinese to restore the deposed Guangxu Emperor and press for constitutional monarchy against the revolutionaries.
Duan Qirui (1865-1936), the Beiyang general who dominated the Beijing government at intervals between 1916 and 1920 and again in 1924-26.
Weiting was Yuan Shikai's courtesy name; to greet the President as 'my young brother' was to pull rank as the elder, the point the author draws out.

ch006.anchor: as Li Yuanhong is called Cen Xilin, and Cen Chunxuan called Li Huangpi
ch006.note: The source has crossed the two nicknames. By the custom it describes, a famous man is called by his native place: Li Yuanhong, from Huangpi in Hubei, was 'Li Huangpi', and Cen Chunxuan, from Xilin in Guangxi, was 'Cen Xilin'. The text pairs each man with the other's sobriquet; rendered here as printed, error and all.

The paper is not confirmed in the standard sources. Kang's documented Shanghai organ after his return in 1913 was the magazine Buren ('The Unbearable'), which likewise preached Confucian revival and monarchy; the Guoshi Bao attributed to him here is uncorroborated, and may be a confusion with it. (Uncorroborated: Chinese Wikipedia, Kang Youwei.)

The twelve-day coup of July 1917 in which the queue-wearing general Zhang Xun briefly put the boy emperor Puyi back on the throne. Kang Youwei joined it and was named to a court post; it was crushed within days.

ch006.anchor: the premiership of the puppet state
ch006.note: The 'puppet state' is Manchukuo, the Japanese-run regime set up in the northeast in 1932 under the same Puyi. The gibe, that the monarchist Kang would have made its premier had he lived, dates this sketch to 1932 or later, a few years past the collection's 1933 imprint.
Li Shicen (1892-1934), philosopher, editor and popularizer of Western thought; 'the late' places the writing near his death.

ch007.note: Chen Bulei (1890-1948), the most famous of the Tianduo Bao alumni: a gifted essayist who became Chiang Kai-shek's confidential secretary and chief ghostwriter, and killed himself in 1948.
Li Huaishuang (1874-1926), journalist and poet of the revolutionary press.

ch008.note: The soldiers' revolt at Wuchang on 10 October 1911 that began the Xinhai Revolution and brought down the Qing; the date is now China's 'Double Tenth'.

Xu Zhenya (1889-1937), among these staff writers the most celebrated: author of the hugely popular tragic romance Yulihun (Jade Pear Spirit) and a leading light of the 'Mandarin Ducks and Butterflies' school of fiction. Several names in this list (Wu Shuangre among them) belong to that same literary set.
That is, in the calligraphic style of Su Dongpo (Su Shi), the Song master, whose rounded, full-bodied hand was widely imitated.

ch009.anchor: one of the "Six Gentlemen of Hongxian."
ch009.note: The famous 'Six Gentlemen' of the monarchy movement were the members of the Chouan Society (Yang Du and others), who lent it a scholarly front; Xue Dake, the newspaper propagandist of this chapter, is not usually numbered among them, and the author is using the label loosely for the monarchy's promoters.
The Shanghai Yaxiya Ribao (Asia Daily), the chief Chinese-language organ of Yuan's monarchy movement in the lower Yangtze.
See the Glossary: the lane off Nanjing Road where the newspaper offices clustered, so that to plant a paper there was to plant it in the heart of the Shanghai press.

Yuan Shikai proclaimed himself emperor under the reign-title Hongxian ('Grand Constitution') for the year 1916; a dating like 'the first year of Hongxian' on a masthead was thus open flattery of the new dynasty.

The National Protection War: in December 1915 Cai E and others in Yunnan rose against the monarchy, other provinces followed, and by March 1916 Yuan was forced to abandon the throne. He died that June.

ch010.note: Libai Liu ('Saturday') was the famous Shanghai fiction weekly that gave the 'Saturday school' of popular romance its name. The book's date is loose: the magazine actually began in 1914 (with a revived run from 1921); the 'twelve years' reckoning, like several dates in this sketch, points to a time of writing around 1935.

Shenghuo ('Life') Weekly, founded 1925 and edited from 1926 by the crusading journalist Zou Taofen into one of the most widely read magazines in China; the authorities suppressed it at the end of 1933, the 'suspension' the author notes below.
Shiritan ('Ten Days' Chat', styled in English 'Decameron') was a literary ten-day magazine run by the poet and publisher Shao Xunmei.
Shao Xunmei (1906-1968), poet, publisher and aesthete, an Anglophile man of letters who sank a family fortune into fine printing and little magazines.
1934 was so dubbed in the Shanghai press for the sudden flood of new periodicals; the label was current at the time.

ch011.note: Shen Zhuowu (1885-1931), a Shanghai journalist and broadcasting pioneer, remembered for having recorded Sun Yat-sen's voice on disc in 1924; his Zhongguo Wanbao (China Evening News) was an early Chinese evening paper. He drowned in 1931.
The Mukden Incident of 18 September 1931, when the Japanese army seized Shenyang and began its conquest of Manchuria; known ever after simply as 'Nine-One-Eight'.

The first Battle of Shanghai, begun 28 January 1932, when Japanese forces attacked the Chinese quarters of the city and were held for weeks by the Nineteenth Route Army; known as the 'One-Two-Eight' Incident.
The Cantonese army whose stubborn defense of Shanghai in early 1932 made it a national hero; its withdrawal in March ended the fighting.

ch011.anchor: After Rehe was seized and Yuguan lay in peril
ch011.note: The next stage of the Japanese advance: Shanhaiguan (Yuguan), the pass where the Great Wall meets the sea, was attacked on 1 January 1933, and the province of Rehe (Jehol) was overrun that March. The near-continuous alarms of 1931-33 are what kept the evening extras coming.
Zhang Zhuping (1886-1936), a Shanghai newspaper and advertising magnate who assembled a syndicate of dailies and news agencies; the Da Wanbao was his creation.
Cai Diaotu, a Shanghai tabloid journalist and editor.
The Da Mei Wanbao was the Chinese edition of the American-owned Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury.

ch012.anchor: The middle stretch of Fuzhou Road
ch012.note: Fuzhou Road, the 'Fourth Avenue' (Simalu) of the International Settlement, was old Shanghai's street of print and pleasure at once: the great publishers and bookshops at its heart, teahouses, theaters and brothels along its length.

ch012.anchor: the Zhonghua Book Company and the World Book Company
ch012.note: The Zhonghua (founded 1912) and the World (Shijie, 1917) were two of the largest Chinese publishing houses of the day; the smaller houses named after them, Kaiming, Beixin, the Crescent Moon and the rest, were the presses of the New Culture movement and its rivals.
The Xinyue (Crescent Moon) bookshop and press, organ of the liberal, Anglo-American-educated literary circle of Hu Shi, Xu Zhimo and Liang Shiqiu.
Rendering yeji, literally 'wild chickens' or 'pheasants', the Shanghai term for the lowest, unlicensed street prostitutes, who solicited in the open; the word recurs throughout the book.
Chungong, 'spring-palace pictures', the standing Chinese term for erotic prints and paintings.

ch013.note: Wenmingxi, 'civilized drama', the early name for the new spoken theater, so called as a modern, Westernized alternative to sung opera; it relied on improvisation from a bare scenario rather than a fixed script.
The reign-period of Puyi, the last Qing emperor, 1909-1911.
The troupe of Ren Tianzhi, whose Evolution Troupe (Jinhua Tuan) toured a fervently revolutionary, largely improvised drama in the last Qing years and the first of the Republic.
The Japanese name Ren Tianzhi took during a spell of Japanese nationality; he was a Manchu bannerman by birth.

The Chunliu She (Spring Willow Society), founded by Chinese students in Tokyo in 1906-07, whose staging of La Dame aux Camelias and Uncle Tom's Cabin is reckoned the birth of modern Chinese spoken drama. The cartoon reproduced in this chapter shows the society's celebrated Tokyo benefit performance of Camille (Japanese Tsubaki Hime).
The premises of S. Moutrie & Co., the British piano and music dealer on Nanjing Road, taken over as a theater.

Burugui ('Better to Have Died') was the Chunliu adaptation of Tokutomi Roka's best-selling Japanese novel Hototogisu; The Jeweled Bracelet and Wang Xifeng Spills the Vinegar (a scene from the classic novel Dream of the Red Chamber) round out a repertory pitched at educated taste.
Henhai ('Sea of Regret'), a popular tragic romance of the Boxer year by the novelist Wu Jianren, here in stage adaptation.
Zhang Shichuan (1889-1953), a pioneer of Chinese cinema who, with Zheng Zhengqiu, founded the Mingxing (Star) Film Company and directed some of the country's first feature films.
Shao Zuiweng (1896-1979), eldest of the Shaw brothers, who founded the Tianyi (Unique) Film Company in 1925, the seed of the later Shaw studios of Hong Kong.
Xu Zhuodai (1880-1958), popular humorist, playwright and 'Mr. Funny-bone' of Shanghai letters.

ch014.anchor: three jiao three fen a dance
ch014.note: That is, thirty-three cents (a third of a silver dollar): a jiao, also called a mao, is a tenth of a dollar, and a fen a hundredth. So the plainer halls charged a dollar for three dances.
Rendering canlu shaonian, literally 'pale-green youths', a classical tag for callow, dandyish young men.
Rendering mihun zhen, a 'soul-luring battle-array', the standing figure for a snare that robs a man of his wits.

ch015.note: Roulin, 'forest of flesh', from the classical byword jiuchi roulin, 'a pond of wine and a forest of meat', the debauch of the tyrant-king Zhou of Shang; here it puns on the 'flesh-houses' (肉莊) of the trade.
Xianrou zhuang, 'salted-meat houses', slang for cheap brothels; 'salt-meat' — a preserved, second-rate cut — was the trade's word for a prostitute.

ch015.anchor: the Huang Family Garden in Caojing
ch015.note: A private garden at Caojing, a market town well southwest of the city; a rural spot far from the settlements.

ch015.anchor: past the age of knowing his destiny
ch015.note: That is, over fifty. Confucius said, Analects II.4, that 'at fifty I knew the decree of Heaven' (五十而知天命); 'knowing one's destiny' became a byword for the age of fifty.

Sancun jinlian, the polite name for bound feet, ideally three Chinese inches long. The bones of the foot were broken and folded in girlhood; the mincing gait and tiny 'lotus' were prized erotically, a taste this chapter turns to grotesque comedy.

Women of Yangzhou had a long name in the trade — the city was proverbial both for its bound-footed beauties and for the traffic in 'thin horses' (瘦馬), girls reared and sold as concubines and courtesans.
Lüsong yan, a Luzon (Manila) cigar, an imported luxury smoke.

Gu Hongming (1857-1928), the Western-educated scholar and arch-conservative, was famous for his devotion to his wife's bound feet, which he called his writing 'stimulant' and was said to sniff for inspiration. The author's attribution is apt: CORROBORATED as the standing anecdote about Gu.

ch016.note: Xiao xiansheng, 'little master', a young apprentice courtesan reckoned still a virgin; 'master' (先生) was the courtesy title for a courtesan of the better houses.

ch016.anchor: keep her hidden in a golden house
ch016.note: Cang jiao jin wu, 'to store the darling in a house of gold' — from the boy Emperor Wu of Han, who said that if he could win his cousin Ah-Jiao he would house her in gold; the standing phrase for keeping a cherished mistress.
Qian shuzi, a 'money-tree' that can be shaken for cash whenever wanted; the madams' view of a marketable girl.
Tuoji, to strike a girl's name from the register of the licensed house — the legal act of redeeming a courtesan out of the trade, for a heavy fee.

ch016.anchor: marrying her off with the bud unplucked
ch016.note: Lian bao jia ren: 'bud' (苞) is the maidenhead; the madams' pitch is that the girl goes to her buyer a virgin, flower still folded — for which privilege the redemption price is jacked up.
Shizi da kaikou, 'the lion opens its mouth wide', to name an outrageous, greedy price.
Jian xiansheng, a girl no longer a virgin passed off as a 'little master'; the madams' craft, the text says, could 'mend a broken melon' by artificial means.

ch016.anchor: the jade has come back to him whole
ch016.note: Wan bi gui Zhao, 'the jade returned whole to Zhao' — from the envoy Lin Xiangru, who brought the priceless jade disc back to his king unbroken; the byword for something precious restored intact. Here bitterly ironic.
Meng zai gu li, 'kept inside the drum', the standing idiom for a man kept in total ignorance of what is done around him.

ch017.anchor: she-devils and hags of the coarsest sort
ch017.note: The text names two demon-types: muyecha, a she-yaksha or fury, and jiupancha (Sanskrit kumbhanda), a pot-bellied demon — both stock terms of abuse for a hideous old woman.
Jing'ansi Road, then a lonely stretch running west toward the Bubbling Well temple; now Nanjing West Road, and long since built up.
Sengtu with the contemptuous tu, 'bald-pate'; the sketch turns on Buddhist clergy breaking their vow of celibacy.
Longgong, the jewelled undersea palace of the Dragon King of myth — a grandiose name the author savours for the sordid use it was put to.

ch018.anchor: a byname for a kind of pimping
ch018.note: Lapi, short for lapitiao, 'to pull the leather strap' — to pimp, to procure. The chapter's joke is that a 'harbor pilot' who steers a ship safely into port is here a tout who steers a customer into a brothel.

ch018.anchor: Russian salt-meat, Korean salt-meat, or dwarf's salt-meat
ch018.note: That is, Russian, Korean, and Japanese prostitutes. 'Salt-meat' is the trade's word for a prostitute (see the note at ch015); 'Russian' renders Luosong (from the word 'Russian'), and 'dwarf' (aizi) is a period slur for the Japanese.
The tout's patter uses gualao, a Shanghai pidgin word for a foreign or kept woman; 'Eastern-Ocean' (東洋) means Japanese, 'Russian' (羅宋) Russian.
A street running north out of the International Settlement into Hongkou, with a large Japanese population; the author's 'Street of Mystery' (see ch031).
The main avenue of the French Concession, heart of the White Russian emigre quarter; now Huaihai Road.
A Hongkou street named for the old rifle range; now Wujin Road.
A-Yang-ge, 'Brother Sheep', a type of street sharper; the author gives him a chapter of his own later in the book (ch078).

ch019.note: The licensed courtesan houses ran in three grades. The first and grandest was the changsan ('long three'), where a call and a night each cost three dollars; the second was the yao-er ('one-two'), the subject here; the lowest were the yeji or 'pheasant' houses. 'House' throughout renders tangzi.
Jiaoju: to summon a courtesan from her house to attend a client at a banquet or gaming-party elsewhere — a paid engagement, distinct from visiting her at home.
Da chawei, the daytime 'tea-visit': a client sat a while with a girl over tea and banter for a set fee, without staying the night. See ch021 for the custom in full.
Liu diedao, 'six-and-down', the house nickname for the overnight rate: six dollars the first night, dropping to four thereafter.

ch019.anchor: Slack changsan, rigid yao-er, iron-hard pheasant
ch019.note: A trade proverb (lanwu changsan, ban yao-er, zhu tie beng ying da yeji) contrasting the three grades by character: the first-grade changsan loose and free with their rules, the yao-er rigidly by the book, the pheasants hard as nailed iron over cash. It is here quoted in praise of the yao-er's fixity.

ch019.anchor: prostitution was outlawed by the drawing of lots
ch019.note: Chouqian jinchang: in 1920 the International Settlement's Municipal Council, under missionary pressure, began abolishing licensed prostitution by drawing lots each year to cancel a fifth of the licenses. CORROBORATED (Gail Hershatter, Dangerous Pleasures): the scheme drove the trade unlicensed and pushed many houses across into the French Concession, exactly as the author says.

ch019.anchor: Qipan Street, Cross Street, and Chicken-and-Duck Lane
ch019.note: Streets of the old International Settlement: Qipan ('Chessboard') Street (see ch012's neighborhood), 橫街 'Cross Street', and 雞鴨弄 'Chicken-and-Duck Lane'.

The British-and-American-run concession, governed by the Municipal Council; the French Concession to its south was a separate jurisdiction with its own police, which is why houses fleeing the Council's 1920 ban simply moved across the line.
Yueji, Cantonese prostitutes, whose houses were known for taking payment on the spot in cash.

ch020.note: In mahjong the 'white tile' (白板) is the blank third dragon. To complete a set a player must 'pair' (碰, pung) a matching tile; if two players each hold two blanks, neither can ever draw the pair he needs, and both are frozen — a 'white-tile standoff'. The chapter lifts the term for two clients stuck waiting on one girl.

ch021.note: Zhuang ganshi: the girl set out two dishes, one 'wet' (fruit or the like) and one 'dry' (sweets or nuts), as the token hospitality of the tea-visit.

ch022.note: Jisheng mama, 'Parasite Mama', a demimonde nickname for a procuress; presented by the author as a real figure of the trade.
Xue da kuaitou, a noted Shanghai procurer of an earlier day, as the author reports him; uncorroborated beyond the sketch.

ch022.anchor: took the lead of the pimping world
ch022.note: The text has zhi niu'er, 'to hold the ox's ear' — from the old covenant rite in which the chief of the allied lords held the sacrificial ox's ear; the standing phrase for taking the lead in any field.
Qiong cuoda, a stock self-deprecating phrase for an impoverished man of letters.
Edible swiftlet's-nest and ginseng, the costliest of tonics; the beggar's cry mockingly begs the rich for their leavings of them.
Chi sheng de xiao laopo, a 'leftover little wife' — a cast-off or second-hand concubine being brokered on. 'Concubine' (姨太太 / 小老婆) is a secondary wife.

ch023.anchor: the ninth year of the Republic

ch023.note: Huaxuan or huabang, a 'flower-list' election ranking the city's courtesans by beauty and accomplishment. CORROBORATED as a real Shanghai institution, run from the 1860s onward and by the 1890s staged by newspapers for publicity (the 1897 Youxi Bao and 1917 New World elections are on record); this candy-company version of 1920 fits the pattern exactly.
Qimei milk toffee; the sponsoring confectioner, as the author reports. The stunt — a beauty-poll to sell sweets — is of a piece with the commercialised flower-elections of the day.

ch023.anchor: the Tianyun Tower, the roof-garden of the Wing On Company
ch023.note: The Tianyun Tower (天韻樓) was the roof-garden amusement hall of Wing On, the great Cantonese department store on Nanjing Road (opened 1918); such rooftop 'pleasure gardens' were a Shanghai fixture. CORROBORATED as to the venue.
The 'Electric Light Daily', a small tabloid run by Wu Shuzhen, here made the poll's returning office; no independent record of the paper traced (uncorroborated).
The mock offices — President, Vice-President, Premier — parody the real Beijing republican government of the day, which lends the whole 'Milk President' joke its edge.
A courtesan's professional name: Qinyu is her house, Laoliu 'Number Six' her rank in it. Courtesans were commonly known by such house-and-number names.

ch024.anchor: the first volume of this book
ch024.note: Ben shu shang ji: the author refers his reader to a companion collection where the brothels' technical terms were listed; the present sketches are its sequel.

Chang tanhuang: to promise a client a party and then break the engagement. Tanhuang is a local sung-narrative theatre of the Wu region; 'to sing tanhuang' is to put on a performance, i.e. to spin an excuse.
Chi zifantuan, to dun a client for 'handkerchief-money' (手巾鈿, a tip) at the festivals; the glutinous-rice ball is the festival food, hence the name.
The two characters printed here (接售) are an obscure Wu term of abuse; the exact sense is unrecovered, and the rendering leaves it in romanization.
Tiao laochong: to go carousing at a flower-smoke room (see ch033). Laochong, 'the old creature', is the Wu word for a tiger.
Kai tiaofu, to squeeze a client for something extra; the text notes it is properly thieves' cant (qiekou) borrowed from the street toughs.

ch025.note: Erba, 'twice eight', the standing poetic way of saying sixteen (2 x 8); a girl in her erba is at the age of ideal youth.

ch026.note: Da qiaozi, hoodlums' slang for picking up a woman; 'shell' (殼子) is their word for the woman herself, the objectification the author ends on.

A riddle-saying (xiehouyu) that withholds its point: 'jia, yi, bing...' (A, B, C) leaves the hearer to supply the next, ding (D) — which sounds like ding 釘, 'to tail' a woman. The joke is in the unspoken word.
Meili pai, 'My Dear' / 'Beauty' cigarettes, launched 1925 by the Chinese-owned Hwa Ching (Huacheng) company and the most popular home brand of the day. CORROBORATED.

Qiangdao pai, 'Pirate' cigarettes (British-American Tobacco's Pirate brand, colloquially 'Old Knife', 老刀牌, for the cutlass on the packet). CORROBORATED. A pretty woman rates a 'Beauty', a plain one a 'Pirate'.

ch027.note: The chapter's subject is male prostitution. Tu, 'rabbit', was old slang for a catamite, and 'human rabbit' (人兔) for a male prostitute; the author's disgust is that of his period, and is rendered as printed.
Xianggu and xianggong: the boy-actors of the old theatre, many of whom also served male patrons; the terms had become bywords for a kept catamite.

ch027.anchor: furled their flags and stilled their drums
ch027.note: Yan qi xi gu, 'lower the banners and silence the drums', an old military phrase for a quiet withdrawal; here, giving up the trade.
Duanxiu pi, 'the cut-sleeve fancy', the classical byword for a man who loves men: Emperor Ai of Han, finding his sleeve pinned under his sleeping favourite Dong Xian, cut it off rather than wake him.
Tangbai, the clandestine, unlicensed streetwalkers; the male prostitutes are said to copy their soliciting.
Yao guniang, 'kiln-girls', women of the lowest brothels (yaozi, 'kiln', being slang for such a den).

ch028.anchor: the third of the itinerant trades
ch028.note: The author files hotel prostitution alongside two other trades plied on the move — itinerant massage and itinerant singing — that came to the customer rather than keeping a fixed house.

ch029.note: The fan-seller's cryptic street-cry (wu beng wu shan, shenxian nan bian), roughly 'without the jar, without the fan, not even an immortal can work the trick'; a patter promising a marvel, its exact sense obscure.

The lovers of the great folk-legend: the Herd-boy (Altair) and the Weaving-maid (Vega), parted by the River of Heaven — the Milky Way — and allowed to meet but once a year. An innocent, tender image, here the decoy for the hidden picture beneath.
Yaojing dajia, 'goblins fighting', a common euphemism for a picture of a couple making love.

ch030.note: Ningbo tangzi, brothels run by and for the Ningbo community, then a recent arrival on the scene, operating out of rented hotel rooms rather than fixed houses.

The streets running back from the Bund were popularly numbered as 'Avenues' (馬路, 'horse-roads'): First (Nanjing Road), Second (Jiujiang), Third (Hankou), Fourth (Fuzhou). 'Third Avenue' is Hankou Road.
Shi pu, 'wet berth', a euphemism the text flags as 'to be taken by implication' — a bed used for sex, as against a 'dry berth' merely slept in.

Licensed houses paid a tax and took out a permit; these Ningbo houses paid nothing, so that for all their open trade they counted, in law, as clandestine (私娼) — the same unlicensed category the 1920 lottery-ban had swollen (see ch019).

ch031.note: The two characters are blanked as '××' in the reprint, plainly standing for 'Japanese' (the redaction is the text's own); 'Eastern-Ocean' (東洋) just below means Japan.
The commission was split two-and-eight (erba): eight parts to the house, two to the tout. Note that this 'two-eight' is the ratio 8:2, not the 'twice-eight' meaning sixteen of ch025.
Dapao, literally 'firing the cannon', coarse slang for a single sexual turn.

ch032.note: Baoke, 'the keeper': a man who books a prostitute for his sole use over a long period, paying her whole keep in return for exclusive right to her.
Jinluan, 'the forbidden cut', a private preserve none but the owner may touch; from a Jin-dynasty phrase for a choice morsel reserved for the emperor alone.

ch032.anchor: fickle as willow-fluff on the water
ch032.note: Shuixing yanghua, 'water's nature, willow-flower', the standing idiom for an inconstant woman: water takes any shape, willow-fluff blows any way.

Two pieces of sucker-slang: yuan datou, a 'wronged big-head' or prize fool, and da yangpan, a 'big foreign plate', a green mark easily fleeced — what the girls privately call the keeper who thinks he owns them.

ch033.note: Huayanjian, the lowest grade of brothel, a step below even the pheasant house, where opium ('smoke') and sex were sold together; hence 'smoke-girl' (煙妓) for its women.

ch033.anchor: Lanfang Li, Mill Street, and Dog-Beating Bridge
ch033.note: Old lanes and landmarks of the native city and its fringes (蘭芳里, 磨坊街, 打狗橋), with the Small East Gate (小東門) of the old walled town; the traditional haunts of the cheapest trade.

ch033.anchor: opium boiled up from cheap dross
ch033.note: The 'smoke' was made from the reboiled dross and scrapings of spent opium — the foulest and cheapest grade, whence the text's 'rank smoke'.
Tu lao mazi, a rustic bumpkin newly arrived in the city and easily gulled.

Republican governments repeatedly proclaimed opium prohibition through the 1920s and after; the author notes, drily, that with the smoke gone he cannot say what the houses served instead, and leaves the point blank rather than guess.

ch034.note: Zou jianghu, 'to travel the rivers and lakes', the standing phrase for the itinerant life of fortune-tellers, quacks, entertainers and other roadside trades.
Tianxian huaren, 'a fairy transformed into a mortal', advertising the woman physiognomist's looks rather than her art — which is the author's whole point, that the 'reading' was a sale of charms.

ch034.anchor: the murder of the woman physiognomist Wenying
ch034.note: A Shanghai murder-sensation of the year before writing (the early 1930s), as the author reports it; no independent record traced here, so it is left as he gives it.
Bao ni deyi, 'guaranteed to please you' — deyi, 'to get one's wish, to be well content', carrying a plain second meaning the author lingers over with relish.

ch035.note: The rooftop amusement arcades of the big Nanjing Road department stores, and lesser halls like them, kept female attendants (nü zhaodai, "waitresses" or "tea-girls") to serve the patrons tea. Drawing no wages, they lived on tips and on whatever a smitten customer could be induced to give, and stood on the semi-respectable fringe of the demimonde.
Boli bei (玻璃杯). The tea came in a plain glass tumbler, and the seasoned patrons took to calling the girls by the vessel they carried rather than by name.

ch035.anchor: the Wing On, the Sincere, and the Sun Sun
ch035.note: The three great Cantonese-owned department stores of Nanjing Road — Sincere (先施, opened 1917), Wing On (永安, Shanghai store 1918; its rooftop pleasure-arcade was the Tianyun Tower, noted at the flower-election), and Sun Sun (新新, 1926) — each crowned with a roof-garden of amusements. The dates are corroborated; the rooftop halls were where these waitresses worked.

ch036.anchor: "Born in Suzhou, dressed in Hangzhou, dining in Guangzhou, buried in Liuzhou."
ch036.note: A well-worn proverb (生在蘇州，穿在杭州，吃在廣州，死在柳州): Suzhou for handsome people, Hangzhou for its silks, Guangzhou (Canton) for its food, and Liuzhou in Guangxi for its fine coffin-wood — the four things each place was famed for.

ch036.anchor: a single bowl of shark's fin
ch036.note: Shark's fin, laborious to prepare and reckoned among the "mountain-and-sea delicacies," was the standard centerpiece of a costly Chinese banquet; its price was a rough gauge of a feast's rank.

ch036.anchor: "One feast in a rich man's house, half a year's grain for a poor man."
ch036.note: A common folk couplet (富家一席酒，窮漢半年糧) on the gulf between rich and poor.

ch037.note: Chaizi (拆字), also called cezi (測字): fortune-telling by taking a written Chinese character apart into its component strokes and radicals and reading omens from the pieces — a street-corner divination trade.
Six copper coins (銅板, each a ten-cash piece) made up the sixty cash of the cry. On the money, see the note at the New Year sketch.
Hulu cezi (葫蘆測字), a fancier brand of the same trade under a mystifying name — which let its proprietor charge many times the street rate.

ch038.note: By the author's account a once-renowned courtesan and opera singer, later reduced to singing in the streets. Beyond this sketch the record is thin; the details here are the author's.

Not the heroine of Dream of the Red Chamber but the celebrated late-Qing Shanghai courtesan (1864–1924, born Lu Jinbao) who took that name in fondness for the novel. She was reckoned one of the "Four Guardians" (四大金剛) of Shanghai's courtesans, moved back and forth between the courtesan house and the stage, married many times, and died in poverty — corroborated. Her career is the mirror the author holds up to Weng Meiqian.
Gongwu zhengtang (公務正堂). The courtesan houses aped the plaques of a magistrate's yamen, hanging up mock-official titles on their door-lanterns for show.
Maor xi (髦兒戲), opera performed by an all-female troupe, the women taking every part including the bearded old men. See the last sketch of the book for more.
Xusheng or laosheng (鬚生 / 老生), the dignified older-man role of Peking opera, played in a beard — the role type in which Tan Xinpei reigned (see the next sketch).

ch038.anchor: the seventh year of the Republic
ch038.note: 1918. The book dates by the years of the Republic, which began in 1912.
Xin Shijie (新世界), the large amusement hall opened in 1915 at the corner of Bubbling Well Road — the forerunner of Huang Chujiu's Great World.

ch039.note: Xing shi (性史), the notorious 1926 collection of explicit reader case-studies edited by Zhang Jingsheng (張競生, "Dr. Sex"), a genuine public scandal of its day, promptly banned — corroborated.
Rou putuan (肉蒲團), the celebrated seventeenth-century erotic novel conventionally attributed to Li Yu (李漁, 1610–1680) — corroborated.
Dengcao heshang (燈草和尚), a late-imperial erotic novel.
Xinghua tian (杏花天), a Qing-dynasty erotic novel.

ch040.note: Tan Xinpei (譚鑫培, 1847–1917), stage name Xiao Jiaotian, the reigning laosheng (bearded-male-role) master of his age and founder of the Tan school, the first great school of Peking-opera singing. He died in Beijing in 1917, a few days after being pressed, gravely ill, to perform — all corroborated.

Huang Chujiu (黃楚九, 1872–1931), Shanghai's foremost patent-medicine magnate (the "Ailuo brain tonic") turned amusement-hall impresario, founder of the Great World (大世界, 1917). His career as a theater manager is well attested; his running of this particular house is consistent with it.
Dao hun ling (盜魂鈴), an opera from the Journey to the West cycle. For the star of the bearded-male roles to take the comic part of Pigsy was to play flat against type.
Zhu Wuneng (豬悟能), the Buddhist name of Pigsy (Zhu Bajie), the gluttonous pig-spirit of Journey to the West.
The drama reformer and pioneer filmmaker (see the Glossary and the sketch on the new drama); here he writes as editor of an illustrated theater paper.

The New Stage (新舞臺), China's first modern-style theater, founded in 1908 by the Xia brothers at Jiumudi ("Nine-Mu Land") in the Nanshi district — the cradle of reformed, Shanghai-style Peking opera. Corroborated.

Xia Yuerun (夏月潤, 1878–1931), Peking-opera actor and co-founder of the New Stage. The book's "beloved son-in-law" rests on a real tie: the record names Tan Xinpei as Xia Yuerun's father-in-law — corroborated.

Kongcheng ji (空城計), the famous Three Kingdoms opera in which Zhuge Liang, with no troops to hand, throws open the city gates and sits playing the zither to bluff the enemy general Sima Yi into retreat.
Tan gongfeng (譚供奉). A gongfeng was a performer in imperial service; Tan sang for the court of the Empress Dowager Cixi, and the by-name is genuine.

ch040.anchor: the Boxer troubles of the gengzi year
ch040.note: The Boxer Uprising of 1900, the gengzi year, when the anti-foreign Boxer movement and the Eight-Nation intervention convulsed north China.

Sai Jinhua (c. 1872–1936), the courtesan of Boxer-year legend, popularly linked to the German commander Waldersee. The claim that Tan Xinpei cohabited with her is uncorroborated and looks apocryphal: no standard source records any such tie, and the companion the record does document for those years was the opera amateur Sun Zuozhou, not Tan. The author is passing on gossip.
Zhuzhici (竹枝詞), a folk-song verse form used for topical and local subjects.

ch040.anchor: the whole city vies to speak of Jiaotian
ch040.note: The couplet is real and attested about Tan Xinpei; this second line matches the received wording (滿城爭說叫天兒) exactly. The first line is a variant — the standard form runs "Who can master the rise and fall of states?" (家國興亡誰管得) — and the couplet is commonly attributed to the late-Qing poet Fan Zengxiang (樊增祥).

ch041.note: Hongbang (紅幫) tailors, the Ningbo craftsmen who learned to cut Western-style suits and overcoats for foreign and Westernized customers — "Red Gang" being the trade's name for those who worked for the red-haired foreigners, as against the "Local Gang" who made Chinese dress.

ch041.anchor: the Su and Guang ready-made men
ch041.note: Su-Guang chengyi (蘇廣成衣), the Suzhou- and Canton-style makers of ready-made Chinese clothing (see the later sketch on their shops).

ch042.note: Jiangbei (江北), the country north of the Yangtze around the Subei region; its migrants formed Shanghai's poorest and most looked-down-upon laboring class, filling the humblest trades.
Mai rou (賣肉), the blunt slang for prostitution.

ch043.note: Yeji (野雞), literally "wild chicken" or "pheasant," the Shanghai slang for anything unlicensed, irregular, and fly-by-night — first met as the word for the lowest streetwalkers. A "pheasant university" is thus a degree-mill got up to look like the real thing.
One of Shanghai's two great commercial dailies (see the Glossary).

ch044.anchor: a juren, a jinshi, a Hanlin
ch044.note: The upper rungs of the old imperial examination ladder: the juren (舉人), a graduate of the provincial examination; the jinshi (進士), a graduate of the metropolitan examination held at the capital; and the Hanlin (翰林), the elite academicians chosen from the topmost jinshi — the summit of a scholar's career under the Qing.

ch044.anchor: cutting a slice at the salt-meat houses
ch044.note: Zhan xianrou (斬鹹肉), slang for going whoring at the cheapest brothels; "salt-meat" (鹹肉) is the trade's word for a low prostitute (see the note at the salt-meat houses).

ch045.note: Dujin boshi (鍍金博士), a "gold-plated Ph.D." — a returned student with a foreign diploma but no learning under the veneer, set against the chijin boshi (赤金博士), the "solid-gold" doctor who is the genuine article.
Fengmao linjiao (鳳毛麟角), a set phrase for something exceedingly rare and precious.

ch046.note: Huaping (花瓶), the metaphor — then new — for a woman kept on the staff for her looks, a pretty ornament of no working use, exactly as one keeps a vase in the parlor.

ch047.note: Bao fangjian (包房間), a hotel room let by the year and run as a private gambling parlor (and sometimes opium den) — a club without the club's license.
Rendering quezhan (雀戰), literally "sparrow battle," the common Shanghai term for a game of mahjong.

ch048.note: Baochang Lu (寶昌路), the road's earlier name (given 1906), before its 1915 rechristening as Avenue Joffre. On the avenue itself, heart of the White Russian quarter, see the earlier note; it is now Huaihai Road.

Joseph Joffre (1852–1931), the French marshal who halted the German advance at the First Battle of the Marne in 1914. The French Concession renamed the road for him in 1915, and he attended a formal ceremony there on his visit to Shanghai in 1922 — corroborated.
The First World War (1914–1918), so called in China at the time.

ch049.note: The White Russians (白俄) — anti-Bolshevik refugees who fled the Russian Revolution and civil war, many by way of Siberia and Harbin, to become Shanghai's largest stateless foreign community, thickest in the Avenue Joffre quarter. Numbers of them, formerly people of rank, sank into destitution.

Rendering dingba (釘巴), an obscure term — ding is "to nail" or "to dog someone's steps" — apparently a beggar who fastens onto a passer-by and will not be shaken off. The reading is crop-verified as printed; the exact sense is uncertain.

ch050.anchor: The General Post Office on North Suzhou Road
ch050.note: The head post office (郵政總局), the landmark completed in 1924 at the north end of the Sichuan Road bridge over Suzhou Creek, on North Suzhou Road — corroborated. Its grand second-floor hall was known as the "First Hall of the Far East."
Da yeji (打野雞), "beating for pheasants" — slang for grabbing irregular, catch-as-catch-can day-labor, from the same yeji ("pheasant" = unlicensed, casual) met in the sketch on pheasant universities.
Mianbao wenti (麵包問題), "the bread question" — a period rendering of the Western phrase for the problem of earning one's daily living.

ch051.note: Youbao gongsi (郵包公司), a private forwarding agent that handled bulk parcel-posting for the out-of-town firms' buying agents, who found the post office's formalities beyond them.

ch052.note: Weichun Yuan (味蒓園), the literary alternate name of Zhang's Garden, evoking the water-shield (chun) of the classical tale of homesick longing. Zhang's Garden was built in 1882 by the Wuxi merchant Zhang Shuhe and opened to the public in 1885 — for a generation "the first garden of Shanghai," with theater, teahouse, and photo studio — and closed around 1918; corroborated.

Ankaidi (安塏第), the tall Western-style building that was the landmark and gathering-place of Zhang's Garden, its English name Arcadia Hall. It was pulled down after the garden's owner died in 1919. Corroborated.
Bansong Yuan (半淞園), a riverside pleasure-garden in the Nanshi district, opened 1918.
Kangnaotuo Lu (康腦脫路), now Kangding Road.
Yidingpan Lu (億定盤路), now Jiangsu Road.
Faguo Gongyuan (法國公園), the French Concession's public park (Koukaza Park), now Fuxing Park (see the later sketch).
